source_text:
Ὡσαύτως καὶ διὰ τοῦ λέγειν πάντα τὰ πετεινὰ καὶ πάντα τὰ θηρία νῦν ὑπὸ Θεοῦ πλασθῆναι οὐ δίδωσι ἡμῖν χώραν τοῦ ὅλως εἰπεῖν ὅτι μὲν ἐγένοντο πρότερον, μέρος δὲ νῦν ὅθεν οὔτε περὶ
σπερμοφάγου βρώσεως ἐν τούτοις τι διακελεύεται ὁ Θεός· τὰ γὰρ εἰς παράδεισον εἰσερχόμενα οὐ χόρτον ἐσθίει, ἀλλὰ πᾶν ξύλον ὡραῖον εἰς ὅρασιν καὶ καλὸν εἰς βρῶσιν καὶ πρό γε πάντων ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς Χριστοῦ τοῦ ζωοποιοῦντος καὶ ταῦτα τὰ ζῷα ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἔθνη εἰσὶ ταῦτα τὰ θηρία τὰ ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ συναχθέντα ἢ ὅτι ἱππὼν καὶ συβόσιον καὶ καμηλοστάσιον καὶ οἰοτρόφυον (...) σήμερον ὁ παράδεισος ὑπάρχει. 86 Οὐχ οὕτως, ὦ φιλόσοφε, ἀλλ' ἢ τὸ εἰπεῖν τὸν Θεόν· ἀρχέτωσαν πάσης τῆς γῆς, καὶ τὸ· κατακυριευσάτωσαν αὐτῆς καὶ πάντων τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ, τοῦτο τὸ κύριόν ἐστι τοῦ ποιῆσαι τὸν ἄνθρωπο κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ καὶ ἄρχειν αὐτὸν πάσης τῆς γῆς.
thought_title: The earth-formed animals as nations in the Church, and ruling as the image
orientation: Eustathius is still distinguishing the Genesis 2 animals formed from the earth from the earlier water-born creatures, and now turns to what it means for humanity to rule.
pass_a_gloss: Likewise also through saying that all the birds and all the wild animals now were formed by God, he does not give us room to say at all that some came into being earlier, but a part now; whence neither about seed-eating food among these does God command anything; for the things entering into paradise do not eat grass, but every tree beautiful for seeing and good for food, and before all things from the tree of life of Christ who gives life; and these animals it is possible to say that these wild animals are the nations gathered in the Church by God, or that a horse-herd and a swine-herd and a camel-station and a sheep-fold (...) today is the paradise. Not so, O philosopher, but rather the saying of God: let them rule all the earth, and the: let them have dominion over it and over all the things in it, this is the chief point of making the human being in God's image and of his ruling all the earth.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'formed' for πλάσσω, marking God's direct hands-on action.

choices.english: let them rule all the earth
choices.why: Glossary requires 'to rule' for ἄρχειν; the imperative is rendered literally.
rejected: let them have dominion over all the earth

choices.english: let them have dominion over it
choices.why: Distinct verb from ἄρχω; rendered with 'have dominion over' to preserve the difference.
Glossary requires 'in God's image' for κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ.
κύριον here means the authoritative or decisive point; 'chief point' captures the argumentative force.

bible_refs.note: ἀρχέτωσαν πάσης τῆς γῆς and κατακυριευσάτωσαν αὐτῆς
πᾶν ξύλον ὡραῖον εἰς ὅρασιν καὶ καλὸν εἰς βρῶσιν

pass_b_english: In the same way, by saying that all the birds and all the wild animals were now formed by God, Scripture gives us no room at all to say that they came into being earlier and only a part of them now. For this reason God gives no command among these about eating seeds. The creatures that enter paradise do not eat grass, but every tree beautiful to the sight and good for food—and above all, from the tree of life, Christ who gives life. And it is possible to say that these living creatures are the nations—these wild animals gathered by God in the Church—or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep. No, philosopher, it is not so. No, philosopher, it is not so. Rather, God’s saying “Let them rule all the earth” and “let them have dominion over it and over everything in it” (Genesis 1:28)—this is the chief point of making the human being in God’s image and of his ruling all the earth.
notes: The source contains a lacuna marked by (...) before σήμερον ὁ παράδεισος ὑπάρχει; the gloss reflects only the surviving words.
The numeral 86 appears in the source after ὑπάρχει; it is a section marker, not part of the text to translate.

problems.source_quote: ἀρχέτωσαν πάσης τῆς γῆς, καὶ κατακυριευσάτωσαν αὐτῆς …
problems.why: The cited verse is about ruling, which is Genesis 1:28, not 1:26.
problems.ruling: Source quotes 'ἀρχέτωσαν...κατακυριευσάτωσαν' from Gen 1:28, not 1:26; wrong reference misleads reader.

fixed: The citation for the ruling verses is Genesis 1:28, not 1:26; the source quotes ἀρχέτωσαν πάσης τῆς γῆς and κατακυριευσάτωσαν αὐτῆς, which are from Genesis 1:28.

problems.quote: And it is possible to say that these living creatures are the nations, these wild animals gathered by God in the Church, or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep.
problems.source_quote: ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἔθνη εἰσὶ ταῦτα τὰ θηρία τὰ ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ συναχθέντα ἢ ὅτι ἱππὼν καὶ συβόσιον καὶ καμηλοστάσιον καὶ οἰοτρόφυον
problems.why: Source presents two alternative readings of the animals: nations in Church OR literal beasts; English merges them, losing the disjunction.
problems.fix: And it is possible to say that these living creatures are the nations—these wild animals gathered by God in the Church—or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep.
problems.ruling: Greek gives two alternatives (nation‑beasts OR horse, swine, camel, etc.) without saying 'paradise today'; English adds 'paradise today' merging clauses, altering meaning

edits.old: And it is possible to say that these living creatures are the nations, these wild animals gathered by God in the Church, or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep.
edits.new: And it is possible to say that these living creatures are the nations—these wild animals gathered by God in the Church—or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep.

fixed: The English did merge the two alternative readings, losing the disjunction. The source presents two alternatives: 'ἔθνη εἰσὶ ταῦτα τὰ θηρία τὰ ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ συναχθέντα' (these wild animals are the nations gathered in the Church by God) OR 'ἱππὼν καὶ συβόσιον καὶ καμηλοστάσιον καὶ οἰοτρόφυον' (a literal reading of paradise as a place of horses, swine, camels, and sheep). Using dashes to set off the apposition clarifies the first reading while preserving the 'or' disjunction.

problems.quote: the tree of life, Christ who gives life
problems.why: Sudden identification of tree of life with Christ without prior introduction; reader may miss this is allegorical.

variants.text: the tree of life, Christ who gives life

problems.quote: No, philosopher, it is not so.
problems.why: Reader cannot tell if this is Eustathius addressing his interlocutor or quoting the philosopher's objection.
problems.fix: Clarify: Eustathius rejects literal reading himself.

problems.quote: or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep
problems.why: Sarcastic reductio is grammatically broken; 'or that' lacks main clause, creating run-on from prior sentence.
problems.fix: Repunctuate: 'Shall we say that paradise today...? No, philosopher.'

edits.old: And it is possible to say that these living creatures are the nations—these wild animals gathered by God in the Church—or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep.
edits.new: And it is possible to say that these living creatures are the nations—these wild animals gathered by God in the Church—or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep. No, philosopher, it is not so.

edits.old: No, philosopher, it is not so.
edits.new: No, philosopher, it is not so.

fixed: The identification of the tree of life with Christ is present in the source: 'ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς Χριστοῦ τοῦ ζωοποιοῦντος' (from the tree of life of Christ who gives life). The English renders this accurately; no edit needed.
The speaker is Eustathius addressing the philosopher, as indicated by the vocative 'ὦ φιλόσοφε' in the source. The English 'No, philosopher, it is not so' correctly reflects this. No edit needed.

The sentence structure is grammatically complete in the English: 'And it is possible to say that... or that...' The 'or that' clause is parallel to the first 'that' clause, both governed by 'it is possible to say.' The source has 'ἢ ὅτι...' which is parallel to 'ὅτι...' No edit needed.

last_rejected.source_quote: τοῦτο τὸ κύριόν ἐστι τοῦ ποιῆσαι τὸν ἄνθρωπο κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ καὶ ἄρχειν αὐτὸν πάσης τῆς γῆς
last_rejected.why: Source says this IS the meaning of making man in God's image, not merely the 'chief point' of it.
last_rejected.fix: this is what it means to make the human being in God's image and to rule all the earth
last_rejected.ruling: Greek “τοῦτο τὸ κύριον ἐστι” = ‘this is the main point’; translation “chief point of” matches, not a mis‑translation.
